hand, we don't want people to put themselves in danger. That's not an easy interface for anybody to, to walk. We give people panic buttons to put on their clothing. We've put up mirrors wherever we can put up mirrors so that people can see. So, where they'll operate, we always sort of move them around in order to figure out what the site is that they're going to work the best so I don't have yet the new locations, but we were happy as soon as the additional SHOW vans are on, we'll be happy to provide where it is. We currently have a fleet of six.
Okay. Nice. What is SHOW's total funding in Fiscal 2026?
It's going to increase from 8.3 million to 13 million. And as we just discussed, we're adding three new SHOW vans.
Where will the third new Bridge to Home site be located, and how many beds will be available?
So, we don't yet have the site.
No site.
So, we first have to have the funding. They will never do a program bigger than about 50, just because we think that that's the right size.
That'll work?

Yeah. You want something big enough for efficiency of scale but not so big that it could get out of control, and we think that around 50 is a nice number. You know, I could see us doing something of 40, I could see us doing something of 70, but I can't see 200. So, it sort of depends on the physical structure of the building.
So, since you don't have the location, may I say which Borough at least?
The first one was in Manhattan. So, the plan is for the next two not to be in Manhattan.
Okay.

So, I think I would say Brooklyn and Queens would be very good guesses on where the next two will be or the Bronx, right, so, you know, ultimately we would like to have one in each borough so we would like to grow to at least four, and then be able to have one in each of the

four boroughs. And then we'll see whether or not there's a sufficient need in Staten Island.
Got it. Okay. Are the first two Bridge to Home sites operational, and how would you measure the success of this program?

So, the first one is very operational. We're collecting data now on how many people move into supportive housing. Retention is high, over 90 percent, had very few people leaving, and, you know, to us, you know, what success looks like is that people leave into permanent housing. It could be, you know, supportive housing. It could be that we connect them to their families. It could be, you know, regular housing, depending upon, you know, how they do. What we've seen, and you as a nurse won't be surprised, is that if you give people consistent medication in a supportive environment, they become somebody else, but not immediately. And this is the… in a two-to-three-week hospitalization, all you can do is stabilize someone. You can't really know what their baseline is. To know what their baseline is, you have to give them two to three months of good medicines, good rehab, good

food, right, and then in an environment that doesn't stress them out. And I think what's fun to watch is people are surprised at what happens, even we have seen even cognitive improvements, not just improvements in mental health, but where somebody was using too much alcohol and people said, oh, this person has alcoholic dementia. Turns out if you give them three to four months of good medication, good food in a non-stressful environment, three to four months, they're thinking differently. So, you know, brain, very plastic. Brain can create new neurons and go around the areas that are not working. So, you know, we're very excited that some people are going to emerge different than the way they went in.
Especially the younger folks.
Yes. More plasticity the younger you are.
Does H and H have plans for any additional Bridge to Home site? You said you already have?.

Right. Ideally, you know, I mean, I'd like one in each borough. We would have to approach Staten Island. Sometimes it can be

challenging siting issues, but we will certainly try for one in each borough.
And what data that you use to select the site?

We look for something that's the right size. It has to have both individual rooms because we don't think congregate works well for this population, and has to be some common space and we want it to be near subway lines so that it's accessible to people and acceptable to the surrounding neighborhood.
My question. For the site, do you have… like, you become a tenant or you build from scratch?

We don't build from scratch because it would take too long. We usually look for… well, certainly the current facility, which has worked so well, was once a tourist hotel that ceased to function as a tourist hotel. So, buildings that once functioned as tourist hotels are ideal because they usually have the individual rooms plus the common space, you know, a reception desk, a place to do groups. That's what we… so we need that combination, individual rooms and some common space,

but we don't want to build because that takes too long. That's, you know, two to three years, but if we can rent a space that could be three months.
And which vendors that really operate the Bridge to Home?
We operate the Bridge to Home. I mean, we, Health and Hospitals, we're the operator.
